utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. Today, the 24th of September, 2009. I would like first and foremost to greet the accused, the Defence counsel, all the prominent representatives of the OTP, as well as all the people assisting us in this courtroom. I have two oral decisions to hand down, but before doing so I would like to give the floor to the registrar who has IC numbers to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Petkovic Defence has submitted its response to the Prosecution's objections to documents tendered through Slobodan Praljak. This response shall be given IC1048. The Prosecution has submitted its objections to the list of documents tendered for admission by 3D, 1D, and 4D through witness Josip Jurcevic. This list shall be given IC1049, and 3D has submitted its list of documents to be tendered through Witness Arbutina Alojz, this list shall be given IC1050. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had forgotten my microphone. This is an oral decision relating to the testimony of the expert Witness Milan Gorjanc. In support of a motion recorded on the 2nd of September, 2009, the Praljak and Petkovic Defence have disclosed to the parties and to the Chamber the expert report of their common witness, Mr. Milan Gorjanc. The two Defence teams have indicated that the witness would testify when the Petkovic Defence teams present its case, which they agreed upon. The schedule presented by the Petkovic Defence indicates that this witness should come to testify on the 2nd of November, 2009. The Trial Chamber would like to remind the Praljak Defence that to date -- at that date it will have no time left for the presentation of its case. Therefore, it will not be able to conduct the examination-in-chief of the witness Milan Gorjanc. It is only the Petkovic Defence that will be able to conduct the examination-in-chief. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber that -- reminds you that the Praljak Defence will not be able cross-examine -- to cross-examine this witness insofar as it is one of its own witnesses. When this expert witness comes to testify, it is Ms. Alaburic who will conduct the examination-in-chief. Second oral decision, which relates to time allocation for the testimony of witness Zrinko Tokic on 28th -- from 28th of September to the 1st of October, 2009. According to an e-mail that was sent on the 23rd of September, 2009, to the legal officer, and a copy was sent to the other Defence teams, the Trial Chamber understands that the Petkovic and Praljak Defence teams would like to conduct their examination-in-chief one after the other for one hour and 15 minutes and 45 minutes respectively. This means that the Petkovic and Praljak Defence teams agree to deduct the time of the examination-in-chief and redirect used by the Praljak Defence team from the overall time for the presentation of the Petkovic Defence case. The Trial Chamber therefore decides to accord one hour and 15 minutes to the Petkovic Defence to conduct its examination-in-chief and possible redirect of the witness and decides to grant 45 minutes to the Praljak Defence to conduct its examination-in-chief and possible redirect of the witness. The Trial Chamber would like to stipulate that those 45 minutes allocated to the Praljak Defence will be deducted from the overall time allocated to the Petkovic Defence team. Since the parties have not made any specific request and in light of the subjects to be addressed in the presence of this witness, the Trial Chamber decides to grant one hour to all the other Defence teams to conduct their cross-examination and two hours for the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber would like to specify that the Praljak and Petkovic Defence teams will not conduct a cross-examination of this witness. In short, the Trial Chamber has decided that the Petkovic Defence team will have one hour and 15 minutes, and the Praljak Defence will have 45 minutes. The 45 minutes of the Praljak Defence will be deducted from the time allocated to the Petkovic Defence team. The Petkovic and Praljak Defence teams will, of course, not cross-examine the witness. The other Defence counsel will have one hour, and the Prosecutor will have two hours. I believe that all of this is clear for everyone. In addition, Mr. Stringer has sent us an e-mail indicating that he will be able to cross-examine of -- the expert witness Gorjanc on the 26th of October, 2009.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to you and everybody else in the courtroom. I would like in this open session to thank my colleagues from the Prosecution for investing extra effort to prepare for the testimony of our joint military expert and to enable the Petkovic Defence to start off as they had planned to do with Mr. Gorjanc. Now, I contacted Mr. Gorjanc today and looked into the possibility of going ahead one week in advance, that is, earlier on, and he said that he was ready to come in October. So I'd like to tell you now that we are going to start with our Defence case on the 26th of October. And in conformity with that, we'll be preparing a new list and schedule for our witnesses. So we'll let you know who is going to come into this courtroom to the end of November. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Ms. Alaburic. I would also like to thank Mr. Stringer for having responded so quickly, which enables everyone to work in excellent conditions. There's just one outstanding issue, which is to know whether 3DA, this witness will be coming or not. If this witness comes he will come in the week precedes the 26th of October. If he doesn't come, there's a fair chance that we will have no witness for that particular week. We will wait for the Praljak Defence to tell us exactly how it stands vis-a-vis Witness 3DA. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel, and to everyone else. Just in respect to scheduling, I wanted to inform the Trial Chamber of two things. The 30-day deadline on the Prosecution filing on the expert report of Mr. Gorjanc is next Tuesday, and when we file that on Tuesday, we're going to also indicate to the Trial Chamber how much time we would like to have on cross-examination. So that's going to be coming to the Trial Chamber by Tuesday at the latest. Also, one of the witnesses before Mr. Gorjanc, one of the remaining witnesses for the Praljak Defence, I won't say his name. I think it's public but I'm not a hundred per cent at the moment, so I won't say the name, but I expect that either later today or first thing tomorrow morning we'll send a letter to the Trial Chamber indicating how much time the cross -- the Prosecution would like to cross for that witness. He's a 92 ter witness. He's indicated as a one-hour witness for direct. I think the Prosecution's going to ask for two hours for cross based upon his 92 ter statement, but you'll have that either today or tomorrow morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We shall introduce Mr. Skender into the courtroom. Let me remind you that the Praljak Defence will have one hour, the other Defence teams will have 45 minutes, and the Prosecutor will have one hour and a half. Ideally we should be able to finish the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination of the witness, and the Prosecution could then start on its cross-examination on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Could you give us your first name, last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Zvonimir Skender. My name is Zvonimir Skender. I was born on the 10th [as interpreted] of July, 1939, in Zagreb in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your nationality, or what are your nationalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have dual nationality. I'm both French and Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current position? Are you retired? Do you have a job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are retired from the Croatian Army and the French Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am retired from the French Army and from the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What were your ranks in both these armies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm lieutenant-colonel in the French Army and major general in the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, have you already testified before a Tribunal on the events that unfolded in the former Yugoslavia or are you testifying for the first time today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time -- I'm testifying for the first time today on the events concerning Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read the solemn declaration which the usher is about to show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I declare that I shall tell the truth -- I solemnly declare that I shall tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. You may sit down. General, some information about the way in which this hearing will unfold. You have been called by the Praljak Defence team. You will therefore answer questions which will be put to you by his counsel, Ms. Pinter, whom I'm sure you have met either this morning or yesterday. After that, the other Defence counsel of the other accused who are sitting on your left may put questions to you as part of their cross-examination. General Praljak may even put questions to you of a military nature in the time limit he has been granted. The four members of the bench may at any time intervene to put questions to you, and the Prosecutor, who is on your right, will undoubtedly take the floor on Monday as part of his cross-examination. Had you come yesterday, we could have held our hearing yesterday and today, which means you could have gone home today since you come from Corsica which is long way away. You were unable to be here yesterday. You will, therefore, unfortunately have to stay here over the weekend. Please try and be as accurate as you possibly can when you answer the questions. If there's something you don't understand, please don't hesitate to ask the person who has put the question to you to rephrase it, even if it is a Judge who put the questions to you. If you don't understand the question, please let him know. Everything you are saying is being recorded on the transcript which is on the screen before you. This is -- these are oral proceedings. Therefore, what you tell us is extremely important. The Praljak Defence team will show you documents, and during the cross-examination of the Prosecution some documents may also be shown to you. Today we will have 20-minute break after an hour and a half and resume our hearing again after that and finish at 6.00. Next week, on Monday, we shall start at a quarter past 2.00 and the hearing will end at 7.00 p.m. This is the information I wish to share with you to make sure this hearing unfolds as smoothly as possible so that you can contribute to the truth, General. On Friday and Saturday you will be staying here, and the Trial Chamber orders you not to have any contact with the media or anybody else, for that matter. You mustn't tell anyone, Those are the questions that I've been asked and this is what was being said. You mustn't say anything at all. In addition, there is another something else I would like to tell you, is that you have taken the oath and you are a witness of this Tribunal, and you may not have any contact whatsoever with the Praljak Defence team. Ms. Pinter, I shall now give you the floor so that you can conduct your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to you and all my colleagues in the courtroom and good afternoon to everybody else in the courtroom, especially to the interpreters, who always have a bit of trouble with me, but I'll do my best to be a good girl this afternoon and not go too fast.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General. May I ask you to decide whether you're going to speak Croatian or French, because that will facilitate the work of the interpreters -- or, rather, if you mix your languages, it's a bit difficult for them. I would suggest that you take off your headset while you're listening to me and while I'm asking you the questions, because you'll hear and understand me in Croatian, and you'll understand and be able to hear the Presiding Judge when he speaks in French, and then you can decide. So perhaps that would be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: I shall be speaking French.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. Then take your headsets off.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may I ask the usher to --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry to intervene, but I think it's not proper for the witness to take off his headset so he can at least hear when some other party intervenes in some other language.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what channel is the French on, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that channel 3 is the floor. So perhaps it would be best if the witness were to switch to channel 3, which is the floor, and then he can hear the languages in their original.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, we're going to provide you with the documents now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher help us out, please, and provide the General with the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I've been told that you would be required to put your headsets on and switch to channel 3, please. Thank you. You've now been given the documents, and since that is the case, would you turn to the first document, and it is 3D03710. Do you recognise the document?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I wrote it. I wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It's the statement that you gave to the Praljak Defence. And did you give it to the best of your knowledge and recollections and truthfully?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: May I ask you to wait for me to finish before you start speaking, which gives the interpreters a chance to interpret without any overlapping. So you signed this statement; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The first part of your statement relates to your military education, training, and your experience in the army. Could you tell the Court, please, as briefly as possible, because we've already got it all in your statement, where you were educated and trained and so on?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: I was trained in the Foreign Legion in Algeria. I joined on the 10th of April, 1959. The basic training lasted four months. I then joined a unit which was fighting as part of the Legion. After a few months, I went back for a four-months' training, and I then obtained the rank of corporal. After one year, approximately, I went back for another training course in Algeria and became a sergeant. I was part of a fighting unit until the end of the Algerian war. I then returned to France, more specifically to Corsica, on the 28th of June, 1962.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, you needn't go into the details. We've heard what you've just said. We have the details in your statement. How long were you in the French Army, and what was the rank when you -- your rank when you left the French Army?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: I retired from the French Army on the 17th of July, 1989. My rank was that of a lieutenant-colonel then.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And your military experience and knowledge enable me to ask you the following question: What, according to you, is the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, General, before we address the issues of chain of command. So we know that you were a lieutenant-colonel when you left the French Army. If I understood you correctly, when you joined on the 10th of April, 1959, you were a Croatian by nationality. In the Foreign Legion you acquired French nationality. As one says, in the Foreign Legion, through the blood that you have spilt. When did you become French actually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I became French at the beginning of June 1965.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You entered lieutenant -- as a lieutenant-colonel in the French Army. Can you confirm that your training in the French Army was quite remarkable? You started off as a private, and you were, when you left the French Army, a lieutenant-colonel. That was quite exceptional.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, to be quite frank, this was exceptional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, you were a member of the elite corps, the crack troops.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, could you say it this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: With all due respect, I'm listening to the interpretation, and I'd like to warn the witness that -- or, rather, could -- Witness, could you wait after a question has been posed. And I was asking you about the chain of command. What does the term "chain of command" mean and the concept, and what are the basic requirements for the chain of command to function without a hitch or to function well?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: The chain of command is a chain -- when a commander of a unit gives an order, the order goes downwards, so to speak. In other words, down to the last echelon, i.e., the private. For this to work, it is necessary, of course, to have the right men, those that are used to giving the orders and those that are used to executing the orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can we then say that for the functioning of -- we need a line from bottom to top and from top to bottom? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: In your statement you say that you came to the Republic of Croatia -- well, could you tell the Court when that was and why? When did you come to Croatia and why?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: I arrived in Croatia in June of 1993. There was a Croatian officer there whom I had met in the Foreign Legion, who contacted me and who asked me if I wanted to go and come and give a helping hand to the Croatians to defend their country.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did you stay in the Republic of Croatia for any longer, or did you go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: When I arrived in Zagreb, I knew no one there except this officer who commanded a battalion, and he asked me to -- he allowed me to be billeted with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, when in June you were called by this officer, you got this telephone call from this officer asking you to come, you were under oath and you were telling us that you went to Croatia on your own volition. No one in France told you, "You're needed over there. You must go over there," no one from the secret services, the French Army? Could you tell us whether anyone from the French State intervened to tell you that you must go over there, or is it or is it something you made on your own volition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is something I did on my own volition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the name of this officer who called you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time you were in Corsica, were stationed in Calvi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I lived in Corte, in the middle of Corsica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, you arrived in Croatia. Did you stay in Croatia or did you go elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, on the 5th channel -- [Interpretation] Channel number 5 we're hearing Croatian instead of French. It's the second question from Ms. Pinter which was not translated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: My question to the General was: Could you please answer, General?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: No, I didn't stay in Croatia. I left for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Where exactly?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: In Citluk.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. In order to gain time - there is a lot in your statement - what was the situation in Citluk like when you came there? I'm interested in the military organisation. What was the situation in the HVO at the time when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the counsel is going very quickly, but I believe that we should go step-by-step. Filipovic called you and said, "We need you," and then you left for Citluk in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Could you tell us whether at that time you actually signed a contract with the Croatian Army, or whether you were just a volunteer with a very undetermined status who just went to go and give a helping hand in Citluk? Could you tell us what your position was at the time? Or maybe you had been recruited as a "mercenary."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was not recruited as a mercenary. I arrived in Croatia where I knew no one. I ended up in this barracks with Filipovic. At that moment, Bugojno in Bosnia-Herzegovina had fallen, and someone from the Ministry of Defence asked me whether I would volunteer to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina. I signed no contract whatsoever with the Croatian Army, but I decided to go as a volunteer to help the Croatians in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yourself, did you have any kinship with Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you have relatives over there? Where does your family hail from? Does it hail from Croatia or from Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no connection whatsoever with Bosnia-Herzegovina. My family comes from Zagreb. Well, what's left of my family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So why did you go to Citluk? Why did you go to Bosnia-Herzegovina? What motivated you to go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was motivated because of the problems encountered by the Croatian population. There was no afterthought or -- as far as separation or any other idea. I had -- did not have that in mind at all with Croats on the one side or on another side, whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, my question was this: What did you find in Citluk? What was the situation like in terms of the HVO -- or, rather, the military component of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: When I arrived in Citluk after a long road trip, going through the island of Pag, I was asked the following question: "How can you help the HVO?"

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: They [Previous translation continued]...

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: I believe at the time it was Colonel Matisse. I believe that was his name, or close to that. Not Matisse, Matic. Matic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: There was no command post at the time, or command position, and therefore Colonel Matic asked me to tour, to inspect, if I could say so, the front line and then report to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And what did you establish?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: On the field I found a catastrophic situation. The units were poorly equipped, hardly trained, or very poorly trained. They were all volunteers, and they were commanded by people who had no basic military training.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You said that they were volunteers. Could you please describe a military unit for us when you toured the field and when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: They were organised according to brigades or regiments. Either in brigades or regiments. They were just normal people, village people, or people coming from small towns. They were integrated into these units and sent to the front line. There was a rotation. There was a rotation, usually one-third at a time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And were there any problems with sending people to the front line or whether that was organised well? Was the response good? Could you have troops along the whole front line without any problems?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: The response was -- when these people joined the combat units, it was very difficult for them to be integrated into these units. There were a lot of people absent from the front, but mainly on the front line --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Notably when the front line was far from their own village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These people just didn't like going to fight far away from their village.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to see what the discipline was like among the troops?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: It was hardly -- there was no discipline whatsoever, or hardly any. There were small groups commanded by -- by small little chiefs in such a way that it was very difficult for the unit commander to command these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one minute. These HVO soldiers who were often absent, who were far from their village, there was a total lack of discipline, no training, no military training whatsoever, compared to the situation you experienced during the war in Algeria with the Fellaghas, was there a different nature between those who you fought in Algeria who were civilians with a military command or were these HVO people just plain civilians? They were just given a weapon and a uniform but no military training whatsoever? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were civilians, civilians to whom weapons were given, but they didn't -- there wasn't much command. There wasn't enough people commanding them. Whereas in Algeria, the French Army was organised, trained, and there was no -- there was no command problem. There was no problem regarding the reporting of orders also in the line of command, bottom to top, with reporting. This did not exist within the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question from my fellow Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to come back to the volunteers in the HVO, these volunteer soldiers. You said that in the HVO you met volunteers and small chiefs, as you called them. According to you, is "volunteer" a pejorative or is it positive as far as you were concerned? And in the Foreign Legion you were a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To answer your first question, the volunteers in the ranks of the HVO were civilians. On paper they were part of the military organisation, but only on paper, whereas in the Foreign Legion, the volunteers become professional soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So we talked about the volunteers. Now let's talk about the small chiefs. You know that an army can only work with discipline, and with discipline you have to have sanctions. If you have no sanction, there's no discipline and then there's no army. So you mentioned these small chiefs. Could you tell us whether they would severely punish their soldiers, their volunteers who were under their command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because -- that was the problem. These small -- small chiefs were able to impose their will on small groups, and the unit commanders were almost unable to do anything, because when they -- if they behaved with severity, they might lose a good number of volunteers. And actually, the situation became such -- was such -- became such that each man counted at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you told us that you toured the front line, that according to you the situation was catastrophic. Did you draft a written report on the situation, or did you just report on this orally to those who were asking you about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wrote a number of reports, reports which were addressed to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there you drew -- you told them about the situation, which was very poor, very bad.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the situation, why did you stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was just one additional motive for me to stay, to help out, to help these people out so they could stay on their land, and I wanted to provide them with my military knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We have General Skender's reports, but through my omission they were not put on 65 ter list, and that's why they have not been prepared for this examination-in-chief. One of the reports have already been -- has already been used, and I can give you the Defence numbers for the documents. They have not been put on 65 ter list through my omission.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to refer to your statement in which you describe the situation with regard to reporting along the vertical line up and down, and you say that the situation was very difficult in terms of both control and reporting. You are saying this on page 3D42-5273 of Croatian, and in English it is 3D42-5281. Now I would like to ask you this. The situation was bad and that's how you found it. Your assessment in view of your experience and your stay in that area, would you say that the commanders consciously provided for such a bad situation, the chain of command and the flow of information up and down the chain, did they just simply ignore the facts and issued an order that they then neglected, or is there a third reason why the situation was as it was?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: No, they did not neglect that, but when an order was issued, an order was issued top down, it was very difficult if not impossible to be absolutely sure that this order actually ended up where it was supposed to end up, and it was even less sure to know whether the order hadn't been changed while it was being transmitted. What I mean is the following: When a unit commander said something, issued an order, to be sure that the order was correctly understood, the only solution was for the -- was to directly ask the -- the last addressee of this order whether he obtained the order, and there often there were surprises. Most of the time the order that had been issued, I'm not saying all the times, but most of the times the order that had been issued had changed along the line of command, and the reason for that was that the entire chain of command had been very poorly trained. Everyone would interpret the order according to his own ideas, and there were hardly any contradiction on the way back up. Because of this situation, the command never knew whether the order issued had actually been carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Pinter, that I interrupt you. The general spoke about the implementation of the orders and the difficulties connected to those, to the implementation, and also in his statement there are references to the rules to be followed and -- and at the very beginning of his statement, on English text page 1, second paragraph, there are references to the -- at one of the places to the Geneva Conventions in plural, and then in the end of that very paragraph there is a reference and I quote that: "We are -- that even in harsh discipline environment we are not obliged to execute orders which are not in accordance with the Geneva Convention on -- Convention," in singular, "on human rights." And there are also references to the Geneva Conventions later on. I would like to ask the general, because probably it is a question of translation that there was a reference to the Geneva Convention on human rights that, according to his knowledge and what he learned, what kind of conventions are we speaking of, so what would he recall -- what would you recall about the Geneva Conventions in a more detailed way? I do not say that you have to give us a lecture about the Geneva Conventions, but if you would be able to tell us one or two of those Conventions which you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I don't speak English and I did not get the French translation. [In English] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Well, that's a pity. Of course, really I don't want to take too much time with this question. Let me summarise what I would like to -- to ask from you and give the following: In your statement there are references to the Geneva Conventions and also to a Geneva Convention on Human Rights, but I would like to ask you that as a soldier who was trained in the Foreign Legion, and also you later on took responsibilities in the -- in -- actually in Herzegovina, Bosnia-Herzegovina, what kind of Conventions do you know about when you talk about the Geneva Conventions? In concrete terms what kind of rules you believed that they are contained in the Geneva Conventions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course there are a lot of rules in the Geneva Convention, but for the main part at that time that needed to be applied on the ground were the rules that stipulated that one should not brutalise, kill the prisoners of war of the opponent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, without addressing the legal issue of the Geneva Conventions, when you joined the Foreign Legion, you signed what is called the Code of Honour of any legionnaire. Can you confirm that at the time you joined the Foreign Legion you were shown this code which you signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember that in this code of legionnaires, chapter 7, one mentions this, and I quote: "In combat you must act dispassionately and without hate. You must respect the enemies that have been conquered. You must never abandon either the dead or the wounded or your arms." In chapter 7 there is this sentence: "You must respect the enemies that have been conquered." Since you were a high-ranking officer, how did you understand this when you were in the military in Citluk and elsewhere, this notion of respecting the enemies that had been conquered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is indeed an item in the code of the legionnaires. That is exactly it. When I arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I advocated this to everyone I was in contact with, and I told everyone that the prisoners should not be hurt, the prisoners should not be killed, even less so, because people who do that will be held liable for murder, but after these killings those people will never be able to rest in peace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly, you conveyed this message, and you told these men that they should not commit any crimes. As far as the people under you were concerned, did you remind these men that the Conventions existed that had clear indications of what to do with the prisoners of war? Did you really convey the spirit of the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every time I had the opportunity, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, do you know whether the other commanders did the same? That is to say, did they caution their men about how to behave towards civilians, prisoners of war, and so on, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: I don't know, but what I do know is that I had in my possession a small booklet - I don't know who had signed it - which explained or spelled out the Geneva Conventions. This had been published by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you. Published by the HVO, yes. I'd now like to ask you to open the following document: It is 3D00796. And we'll come back to the situation in Herzegovina where you were. And it's a document dated the 26th of October, 1993. You were shown this document, General, yesterday. I showed it to you; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Could you please give me the number of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D00796. It's the first document after your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: 76. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You've already seen the document. You saw it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Do you stand by what it says in this document, or do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: This is document 5D76, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I think it's difficult for you to find your way around the documents. In the binder which Ms. Pinter has given you, you have small tabs, yellow tabs. You should find this on the second and it, which is dated the 26th of October.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I got it. Yes, I can see this document. I must say that I did not attend this meeting for the simple reason that I was in France for a few days. But on reading this document, I find it quite adequate since a number of questions are put to the Ministry [as interpreted] of Defence. It's quite appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: From anybody else in addition to the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: It's also addressed to the civilian and political authorities, since they are to adopt a series of laws that would enable this proposal to go through.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, from this document may we conclude that the military component of the HVO had problems with mobilisation, or was mobilisation something that did not pose a problem, that the brigades were up to strength and equipped properly? And can we conclude that there weren't too many deserters either, so that didn't pose a problem? Or perhaps there were deserters and that did pose a problem. Which? And can we also say that all the components did their job?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Not at all. There were enormous amount of deserters and a great deal of absenteeism. I could -- this is something I could check myself when I inspected the brigades that were in the south, brigades of the HVO on the military attendance list, and I could also check their presence on the ground. There were huge gaps between the two, huge discrepancies. For instance, there was something like 1.700 men on the attendance list, but it was something like 1.100, in fact. This discrepancy could only be due to the fact that some were deserters or to a high rate of absenteeism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in your written statement there is a short gap which I would like you to fill for us, please. You say in your statement that you became a commander of the operational zone in Tomislavgrad in December 1993. The document we have before us is dated October before you commanded the operational zone. Can you tell us from June 1993 onwards what was your position inside the HVO before the 1st of December, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't in command of anything. I was part of the HVO. I was something of an instructor, save for an emergency, which in fact was the case when the Muslim offensive was launched on the 15th of August, 1993. I was then asked to assume the command and, if possible, to get back onto ground and regain the territory lost by the HVO. This only lasted a few days, and then I was no longer in command until the 20th of December, 1993, when I assumed the command of the military area in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 15th of August, during this military operation, where exactly did this operation take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] South of Mostar, around or close to the Neretva and the Buna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between June and December, did you have an opportunity to meet the commander of the HVO, who was General Petkovic, who was then replaced by General Praljak? Were you in contact with these two generals at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no contact with General Petkovic, because he was almost all the time in contact with representatives of the international community. General Praljak, well, I saw him for the first time by the by in Prozor. This only lasted a few moments. We didn't even introduce each other, didn't -- however, I met him on the ground in the battle-field in this area between the Neretva and the Buna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you acted as an instructor, what were people saying in the HVO about the command? Who was the commander? The commander -- who was the commander? Was it General Petkovic, was it General Praljak, X, Y? What did people say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- I can only say that General Praljak --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying that General Praljak was very much liked by his men. General Petkovic, a little less so, despite the fact that he was my friend, because people at the time did not like the officers that came from the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were on the ground, General. From where you were, did you have the feeling that the supreme commander was Mate Boban, or the defence minister, or the commander of the HVO, or no one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had the feeling, and I am practically sure that everything had to go through Mate Boban. But I cannot vouch for it 100 per cent, because I have no proof of it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Since we've just mentioned General Praljak, apart from that meeting in Prozor and in August 1993, did you ever meet him again before you became commander of the Tomislavgrad Operation Zone?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: I was in contact with General Praljak when I commanded the area in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we have a big problem, which is the following: You have just told us that you assumed the command of the military area in Tomislavgrad in December. General Praljak left his position in November. He went to Zagreb then. How can you explain this to us, this discrepancy in the time line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was in contact with General Praljak in January 1994, he was no longer the leader of the HVO, but in light of the huge problems that arose at the time in Prozor, I had asked him to come and give us a hand to try and find a solution to this problem which was a serious one, since he knew the men who were there and the men who were there knew him, and he was well-respected. He agreed to come, because at the time he was in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we found a solution to this serious problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, what we knew so far is this: That General Praljak left his position as the commander of the HVO at the beginning of November, the 8th of November. He goes to Zagreb, and he then seemingly has a hard time for a short while before emerging on the scene again as a close aid of President Tudjman and as a military advisor. We have seen material evidence of this, that he re-surfaces again afterwards. In January 1994, he is no longer part of the HVO and does not figure anywhere on the administration files of the HVO. When you saw him again or when you saw him, how was he? Was he dressed as a civilian, as a military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, he was dressed in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly, he came to give you a helping hand to solve a problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite right. This was something he did on a personal note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is something which is normally done in such a situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but it was important to calm things down. The people involved in all these problems were having difficulties. The tensions had risen very high.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And was your command of the HVO aware of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I believe so, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Since we're at this point, General, could you describe what the situation was like when General Praljak was called to come and give his assistance, and could you tell us the period of time that this happened?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: This had to do with a very serious incident. This occurred towards the end of January. I can check the dates. In the town of Prozor, there were people who were drunk, and two killings occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Just one moment. Are we talking about HVO members -- or, rather, Croats, or are you talking about an event where both the Muslims and Croats took part?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about an incident that occurred between Croats of the HVO. Let me specify. This had to do with men from the Rama Brigade and soldiers or men from a brigade that came from Bugojno. Two men from the Rama Brigade were killed in a bar, which gave rise to the withdrawal of a great number of the military in Rama on the defence lines, and they started moving towards Prozor. On the other side, the military that were part of the Bugojno Brigade did likewise. The men from the Rama, from Rama surrounded the command of the area -- or, rather, the area of my command. Prior to that, I arrested and made sure that the man who was suspected of having killed these two men was protected in a shelter -- who was suspected of having killed. It was clear that there had been this conflict between the two brigades. This would have affected the whole area. The Rama Brigade, in other words the men -- the military from the Rama Brigade, then demanded that I hand over this man from Bugojno, which I refused to do, because I knew full well that if I did that, that man would be a dead man. Given that the situation was so serious, we decided -- or, rather, I -- I appealed to General Praljak, I appealed to the military police and to a military judge in Livno, and in addition I appealed to a number of prominent political figures. The situation calmed down, and after having provided guarantees to the men of the Rama Brigade that this man would be tried according to the law, and that's what happened. It took a good 48 hours for the situation to calm down a little.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did General Praljak manage to calm the situation down? Was he involved in that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Yes. General Praljak played the most important role in defusing the situation, given, as I said, that the men knew him and he knew his men. He knew these men.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You said that you had seen General Praljak in Prozor and that you had also seen him near Mostar in the month of August. Did you meet him in the Main Staff as he well? When you arrived you were in Citluk, in the Main Staff, as you've told us.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: No. I never met him at the Main Staff. I was on the field every day. And when I went to the Main Staff, he wasn't there. I guess that he was doing the same as I was. He was also on the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we have heard a good number of witnesses, and we've also heard General Praljak. He sat in your seat just a few days ago. We understood that in the HVO there was the Main Staff and the operational zone commands, and you, for example, were commander in December of the Tomislavgrad command. Now, this is what I would like to know, because you are the first one that we have who is right under the -- you're the first that we have that is right under the HVO command. I'd like to know whether the three Cs, the C cube -- the C cube was always enforced in the Main Staff, and I would like to know whether there was always someone on duty at the Main Staff who would be totally always in contact with the duty officer in the operational zones. I'd like to know whether there was a permanent communication between these duty officers, because you've just told us, "I went to the Main Staff and he wasn't there." Fine, but I guess there must have been a duty officer there. And in your own operational zone, there was also a duty officer. At least I guess so. Was that the way things worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Each staff or military region or operational zone had a duty officer, and these duty officers were always in contact with each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So communication between the Main Staff and the operational zone was ensured round the clock.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I believe it's time for the break, or our only break. It's 10 to 4.00. We will now break for 20 minutes. Therefore, we will resume around 4.10 or 4.15, and we'll run until 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, in response to a question from Judge Antonetti about whether communication between the Main Staff and the zones were constant and secure, your answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And in that communication there was no problem either with respect -- either from the operative zone to the Main Staff or vice versa, from the Main Staff to the operative zone; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now would you look at the next document, and as Judge Antonetti told you, you have a yellow sticker where it says 3D01098. Have you found the document? It is dated the 11th of September, 1993, signed by someone for Slobodan Praljak. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: 98. Yes. September 11, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, according to your military experience, is it customary for a Main Staff commander to write "urgent" on these reports?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: No, this is not customary. Normally when a commander issues an order, the order is carried out, but in this document I see that he's asking to be told quickly why the order was not carried out, which proves once again that the chain of command did not work from top down.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may. Witness, you say that this shows that the command chain did not operate properly, but if I understand you correctly, this means that a communication was not transferred or transmitted at one point in time, but maybe another is -- another solution is that the Livno Command forgot to answer, so it would be a communication problem but a discipline problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't say what it was. I cannot be sure that the communication was actually transmitted. But I believe that the order was not carried out, and there was no -- but it wasn't carried out and there was no report on why it wasn't carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I see that you agree with my observation, which says that there are several possibilities to be envisaged here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in -- as far as HVO is concerned, you're the first commander of an operational zone to come and testify. So far we have seen no one at your level, which is why it's extremely interesting to have you in the witness box, and this gives us the opportunity to put a number of technical questions to you. When we look at this document, which is issued by General Praljak as the HVO Main Staff commander, when this document arrives in the operational zone could you tell us whether the operational zone commander is going to read the document himself and maybe put some -- mark it and then issue orders, or is it his assistants or someone else who is going to receive the document, which means in that case that the operational zone commander might not see this document. Could you tell us whether the military rule is that all orders coming from the top must be read by the people under the superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document must have been read by the commander of the operational zone. He was the -- he was to receive this document, because the Livno Brigade is under the command of the Tomislavgrad Operational Zone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or military region, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why the commander of the region did not react before he -- General Praljak reacted, because he should have been the first one to react.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me give you an example. Let's say that the commander of the military region is not at his desk. He's touring the front. He's inspecting a unit. A very urgent order arrives coming in for Mate Boban, for the Ministry of Defence, or for the commander of the HVO, personally sent to the commander of the operational zone. The duty -- what should the duty officer do in such a case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The duty officer is first must write down this document in the logbook, then secondly, he must contact the commander of the regional district to which this order was sent in any kind of fashion to make sure that the region commander can read the document and then react.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Another technical question but the last one. The commander of the military region, let's say you, for example, in December, you arrive at your desk in the morning. Are you going to take a look at the logbook to see what exactly happened overnight? Is it something that you do customarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because I was trained to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: According to your personal experience while you were the advisor, while you were not appointed in official terms in the HVO as commander of the operative zone, did you come across situations in which you were able to see what the commanders' of the operative zones conduct was? Did they look at the various books and logbooks and so on? Do you have any knowledge about that? If not, you needn't speculate or guess.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: No. I don't know exactly whether all operational zone commanders worked as I did because I wasn't there when they arrived and took over their regional command.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, do you know the following: General Praljak was sitting in the HVO HQ, in the command, from, say, July 1993 when you were in the area of Herzegovina. Was he there, or he went to Zagreb, or was he up at the front line or was there some other explanation as to where he was which explained why you couldn't meet?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: I said that I met General Praljak twice on the field, once in passing in Prozor at the end of July, and a second time in the middle of August during the operations to recapture the terrain lost by the HVO between the Neretva and the Buna. I didn't know where he was apart from these two times.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Was it normal for General Praljak as the commander of the Main Staff of the HVO to be on the front line?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: No. But if you want to know exactly what's happening, you have to go -- that's the way -- that's what you have to do. As I said earlier, to know exactly what is happening, you have to go on the field to check what's happening, which proves that the report chain didn't work well from bottom up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: In this courtroom we also heard that General Praljak spent most of his time in the months of July, August, and September on the front line. What you're saying is that that was the only possible -- possible way for him to work, or do you think that he had to act differently in order to provide for the three Cs, the command, control, and information?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: As far as I know, General Praljak likes direct contact. He'd rather go for human contact, and he always wanted to prove, to show to his men on the field that he was with them, amongst them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: How did it reflect on the foot soldiers? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Excellent, as far as the morale was concerned. Men on the field liked to see their commander with them in the same quagmire, if I could say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: According to what you personally experienced and saw in the territory of Herzegovina, was that the only possible way to have an insight into the entire -- into the whole situation, or was there any other mechanism in place? Was that only because General Praljak had felt the need to be in contact with his men, or was it just a necessity?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: General Praljak liked this kind of contact, but it was also a necessity. The morale of the troops was a bit low. But every time a commander would come to visit the men and to get direct information from them, that way he could get a better idea of what was happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you -- if I may, Ms. Pinter. What you're telling us is not new. We've heard about this already. However, I would like to know what was the relationship between this commitment on the field, which is probably extremely positive, as you just told us, and the tasks of a commander when he's in his headquarters. Do you know how General Praljak maintained contact with the headquarters when he was touring the front?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but I guess that the front was never too far away. So it didn't take a long time to return to the Main Staff, to the HQ, where meetings were probably held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, but this is a bit -- this conjecture is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] No. No. Look at the front line. The front line at the Neretva and the Buna, they were just a few kilometres from the Citluk HQ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not where I see you giving us a hypothesis. You said, "I suppose the front was not long. I guess the front was not long -- far away."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Far away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then you said there were probably meetings at the HQ, probably, which means that it is not something you know for sure. You're just supposing that that's the way things happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, which is why I added this probably. I wasn't there. I'm not 100 per cent sure that these meetings were actually held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in the same line of questioning regarding this problem with communications, if I understood you correctly, in August, around August 15th, you came to help in the framework of this military operation on the Neretva-Buna front, and if I understood you correctly, you saw General Praljak on that occasion. Now, when you saw him, in August he was -- he's just taken command of the HVO. So he's the number one in the HVO. He's the number-one man. And when you saw him, could you tell us whether he was escorted by a de'conte [phoen], a transmission man, someone that would be equipped with a radio set to make sure that the connection remains with -- the [indiscernible] connection with the HQ, whether he's coming with a vehicle that has a radio set, you know, so that there's continuity in the chain of command and communication with the chain of command. Can you tell us whether you remember whether this was the case or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember this very well. It was at night, and he came alone. His vehicle was not very far away, but I don't know whether there was a radio link in this vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in an army worthy of this name, could you -- can one consider that the number-one man, the commander, would go and tour the front line, go -- without any logistical support with him so that he can continue to control all the operational zones under his command, or could this be the proof of a certain amateurism in the forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In all force -- armed forces it's absolutely impossible for a commander no longer to be linked to the staff. If this happens, this is very serious. However, in a combat -- in the context of the combats that were going on in these areas, this was not of major importance after all, because there was the duty officer and the assistant commander who were there and who could always take over. And then on the other hand, I think that General Praljak, like everyone knows, was not trained as a military, so he acted -- I don't want to say as an amateur, but he wanted to go and tour the terrain to see what was happening at all times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's continue with this line of questioning. Do you have any idea of how informed General Praljak was as far as what was happening in general in other places than where he was? Did he have an overall view of the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question on this topic, but before answering, please be very careful about my question. We know that you were on the field as early as June 1993. We know that you took command of an operational zone as of December 1993. We know, because you told us, that you took part in military operations, in combat operations, in August, for example. Now, here's my question, and it's very important, so listen carefully: At your level, did you feel -- did you get the feeling, or were you sure that everything that was happening militarily was militarily controlled from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because the operations that were under way in the area were local operations. Now, whether Zagreb was told about it or not, probably so, but I can't vouch for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A follow-up question: While you were in command, in your own HQ, did it ever happen that you received a call from Zagreb, either by phone or called through the radio or through another way, asking you to report on such-and-such situation or such-and-such problem? Did this ever happen to you? Remember that you are under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It never happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're absolutely sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A hundred per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, can one say that the HVO as you found it when you came there was an organised army?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: It was an organised army but poorly organised. There had been a call-up so that men were sent to the front lines, but this call up had been poorly done, because as I told you, there was a huge amount of absenteeism. You could see that the training also very poor. Of course, with time it improved slowly, but this was a far cry from an effective and professional army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, whether that was the -- because there was no wish to organise the army or was there any other reason why the situation was as it -- as you found it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: No, this was not deliberate, but have a well-organised and well-trained army, it takes more than a few months or even a few years. It takes years and a lot of work to make sure that you end up with a well-trained army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And what was the role of the war in establishing that army? How did the role affect the whole process?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: It only made the process worse, because this new army had to be set up and developed while combat were under way, and it was a tall order for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: In your statement you speak about an event after you were appointed the commander of the area of Tomislavgrad. Before I put my question to you, can you remember when that happened? When did you become the commander of that area?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I assumed command on the 20th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I received a message from the General that he has some military questions to put to you closely tied to military issues, that is, but before the General stands up, I have one more question. General, could you please describe for us the situation when you were personally arrested, the event that you mention in your statement and that involves and has to do with Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite right. This event took place around the 10th of January, I believe. It might have been the 12th of January, 1994. I was in the refectory. I was eating in the refectory. There were a hundred or so men, military men. At some point in the refectory, right at the entrance, there was an armed man. As soon as he entered, he started shooting with his assault rifle. He started aiming at the ceiling, and while so doing asked kill Skender [as interpreted]. Given that the situation was dangerous for me and since I didn't know what this was all about, I answered and I said, "It's me." He was very excited and starting shooting again. He captured me and took me to the command of the Rama Brigade. He forgot to take my pistol away from me, which meant that I could kill him any time I liked. Since I didn't know what all this was about yet, I preferred to wait and see. Once I got to the command of the Rama Brigade, I was asked, "What is all this about? This man was involved in a brawl in town, disarmed, and somebody has taken his pistol away from him." While this happened, somebody told him that this was an order that had come in from Colonel Skender. In the meantime, the brigade commander of the Rama Brigade arrived. He brought this man along with him. Obviously the man was drugged, and he tried to calm him down in another room. I don't know where that was. I then returned to my command where I went on with my work. Now, I then reflected on it and said to myself, What do I need to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we lose the relevant passage before the General goes on to describe what he did next, line 23 where it says, "... and while so doing asked kill Skender," I think I'm right in saying that the General said in French he asked "Who's Skender." So I just thought I'd clarify that before we lose it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time it was out of the question of just not dealing with this. The question for me and the most important one for me was what will happen if I send this man to gaol -- to gaol. The situation was so serious in this particular area that every man was needed. If I locked this man up, for sure 20 or so of his camp comrades would leave the front line, or to avoid this happening, I could just delay him being prosecuted by military tribunal. And from what I learned afterwards, this is in effect what happened. He was tried by the military tribunal a short while after my departure when I left for Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, what you've just told us by quoting this example, well, General Praljak has told us the same thing. In a given military situation, the command must assess the pros and cons, and sometimes notwithstanding the fact that an incident has occurred, a crime has been committed, even a serious event, it is important to consider the military situation overall, not to react instantly, and wait for the right time before doing something. Is this what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right, Your Honour. It was important to analyse the situation and take a decision which would harm this particular area not too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a question which I wanted to put to you right from the start. Let me remind you that in the HVO structure you were placed immediately under the command of the HVO command because you were commanding an operational zone. I'm quoting a textbook example. This is a purely theoretical example. When the commander of an operational zone realises that his soldiers have committed a crime, for instance have burnt a house, have stolen things, raped women, when a commander realises this, what does he have to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in cases like these, the military commanders must quite simply refer to the military police, who will then pursue the investigation to try to shed some light on this or to find the culprits. If this happens behind the front line, it's the military police who is working together with the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your area were you confronted with this kind of situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When I was surrounded by the Rama Brigade, not me personally but my command, I then called the military police. They came in fairly quickly, and they in turn surrounded the Rama Brigade. The military police did the work, shed some light on who was responsible and where this had happened, and the military police then strengthened the military police in the area and reinforced it with extra men to make sure that similar things could occur again, which was a very good thing since the situation improved in all areas in this district.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You quote the case of the Rama Brigade. We have seen a number of documents drafted by the SIS, which indicated that as far as the Rama Brigade was concerned, at some point the military police was corrupt. They -- or the military police abused people. In this situation what must a commander of a brigade do, and what must a commander of an operational zone do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You must know that at that time there were two kinds of military police, one which was a military police of the brigade, i.e., the military of the brigade, and the military police, if you like, the real military police that came from outside. The commander, if he heard about the abuses committed in the area, always called up the real military police, so to speak, and the men that were part of the military police in the brigade, well, everyone knew, and this was something which the SIS was very well informed about, were the first people to commit blunders. After that, the real military police took over and it was reorganised. I can't give you an exact date of when this happened, but the military police in the brigade disappeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
