utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak described the following situation to us: Being made aware of crimes committed by some of his soldiers, being made aware of the front line, to protect the front line it was important not to arrest the culprits, the soldiers, and he rather let things be, because if he had arrested the culprits, there would be fewer men on the front line, which would have enabled the enemy to make a breakthrough. In that case, the enemy could have occupied that territory. In short, make sure that military discipline is respected through arrests of the culprits, but on the other hand, make sure that the front line is sufficiently manned. Well, he had rather make sure that the front line was properly manned. You as a professional, what is your view on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In an organised army, I would arrest this man who has committed some kind of crime. I analysed the situation, and I delayed the arrest for my part and those individuals were tried by a tribunal, to maintain the situation on the front line, which was somewhat urgent and postpone the arrests and prosecution before a tribunal which would rule on the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, as far as the Praljak Defence is concerned, you have five minutes left. A member of the Bench would like to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has to do with the situation which we have talked about and you have talked about. I would like to have your view on the areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was talking about the area of responsibility of a commander. A military commander, is he responsible for what is happening in an area which is the area he is commanding, or is his responsibility limited to a small part of the area? In other words, the area where the front line is located. I hope I have been clear. Otherwise, you can ask me to clarify, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Military commanders are responsible for their area of responsibility where they are fighting. They are responsible for the front line. Anything which might occur behind these lines in the towns or villages must be dealt with by the military police or the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On military maps, very often a circle is drawn around a terrain which is the area of responsibility of a commander. Are you saying that the commander of this area should only deal with the front line and is not responsible in any way for what happens in the rear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A military commander is only responsible for the front line, because let me repeat, behind the front line it is the military police and the civilian authorities that are responsible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said a while ago, General, that if you were a commander and if crimes were committed by soldiers, you would have these men arrested. To me, there is a contradiction here. If this has nothing to do with the commander, why would the commander deal with such a situation? He would let the military police deal with it, because this does not seem to be what you are telling us. It doesn't seem to be your view here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said that I would arrest the military who have committed crimes, this means that these men moved towards the front line or came back from the front line and went home. So long as they're not at home, it is for the commander to make sure that everything is working out properly. And if they are at home and if they are armed, then it is for the military police and the civilian authorities to take over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say I don't find your answer very convincing. I shall not take it any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you have told us that you exercised your command in Algeria. I'm trying to establish a comparison to try to understand clearly what you have said given that there is something a little bit unclear. When you were in Algeria, when soldiers committed offences, when French soldiers committed offences, was it for the commander to arrest these men, or was it for the military police - in that case it must have been the gendarmerie - and the civilian authorities to do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the war in Algeria, it was maintaining law and order that we were involved in, and in all the units on the ground, there were the gendarme who are entitled to act and deal with both the military police and the civilians. In cases where people may -- when outlaws were taken prisoner, as we called them then, or civilians, the gendarme then moved in, i.e., the military police, then dealt with these men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the case we will have to try and in this case which we will have to deliberate on is an important issue of the role of the military commander. Now, if we take the case where you -- there is a front line, which you have just explained to us. So there are HVO soldiers on the front line, but let's say this is an area in which there are civilians, and these civilians are victims, are the subject of offences or crimes. Let's assume that civilians are 4 to 5 kilometres away from the front line and that soldiers going to the front line then rob the civilians on their way to the front line. The military commander who hears of that, well, is he responsible for this? Should he arrest these men and prosecute these men, or should he inform the military police, the real military police, as you say, so that it can conduct an investigation? Must he inform the civilian police or the civilian prosecutor of the locality in question, or the military prosecutor who may refer it to an investigating judge? What should a military commander actually do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A military commander must call the military police and ask it to investigate the matter. The military police would then refer it to the civilian authorities depending on the situation -- depending on the situation. Whether this leads to anything, we don't know, but the commander must refer all these cases to the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question. In this situation you experienced since you were on the ground, when a Muslim civilian, or a Serb civilian, to be precise, was the victim of acts committed by your own soldiers, what were you to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had to act immediately to stop this from happening and to call the military police to refer these cases to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the rule.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if a military commander doesn't do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, he is a culprit since he has not called the police who are in charge of these matters. That means he has hidden something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the case when a military commander knows that an offence has been committed, but he believes or he has some idea that the SIS or the military police is going to handle that, in that case the military commander does nothing and continues business as usual even if he assumes that the SIS or the military police or the civilian police is going to do something about it. Should he not make sure that something is being done about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He should. It's important to check this and to check what is going to happen after that, because after all, it is his soldiers who have committed these offences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the military commander must check and understand what the follow-up to it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He should at least be informed about what happens after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my mind your answers are very clear. I don't see what other questions I could put to you. Let me remind the Praljak Defence that you have five minutes left. General Praljak, you have five minutes to put your questions to General Skender.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General Skender.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Just a few questions. From the moment you arrived in Herzegovina, at least until I didn't go, did you see or take part in any offensive plan, the elaboration of any offensive plan either vis-a-vis the BH Army or the Army of Republika Srpska, or do you think that throughout the time we were on the defensive?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: As far as I know, we were always on the defensive, at least as far as the southern front is concerned. The only offensive operations were planned in January 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question: You moved around nonstop. Did you ever see with your own eyes any one of your soldiers, except for the violence against you, but did you see, not that you were informed but you saw with your very own eyes anybody rape, kill, set fire to, or in any other way violate any international rules and regulations on warfare?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that this information always reached you subsequently from certain sources? Some -- one wrote a report, someone provided information, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Praljak. This is not a correct question, because you have not -- first you must ask whether there were such informations, and then you can ask where they come from. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Well, Judge Trechsel, we know that there was information like that. Information did come in of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Anyway, did you in one way or another -- or let me ask you, how many times did you receive an official piece of information that such-and-such a soldier at such-and-such a police at such-and-such a time committed some violation of the international -- of international war law? Throughout the time you were -- that you were there, did you ever receive a report like that, a piece of paper to that effect?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A follow-up question. I believe unless I'm wrong, and if I'm wrong please tell me so, I think that your former comrades of the Foreign Legion were in Vares. Right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if they were in Vares. However, I know that they were in the Croatian Army, under the command of Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But I'm talking about the legionnaires who were part of the UNPROFOR, of the United Nations forces. Were you in contact with the UNPROFOR? Did you have any contact with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as General Praljak was saying earlier, did these people tell you, "We've heard about this or that, this problem, this abuse that had been committed here, this crime committed here or there"? Maybe hearsay only, but did they relay the information to you? And then what did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They never put this question to me, but let me give you an example. During the offensive in January 1994, during the combats a captain visited me. It was a friend of mine. I knew him. We'd been lieutenants together, and he asked me whether he could visit Here combat zone. I said -- told him that he could, and I even provided him with an escort so that he could see exactly this place where the combat was occurring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: From of what you've said, General Skender, may we conclude -- or, rather, tell me did you ever, while you were in the HVO, receive information -- were you given information, did you have it in your hands, in which you had exact information, exact data, about somebody at a specific time in a specific place having committed violations which go against the rules of warfare? Did you have a report like that in your hands, and then did you say, "Act in such-and-such a way," according to the rules of service? Were you ever handed a report like that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: I never had any written document to this effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I mean a document which your subordinates would hand to you on the basis of which you could act. Did you ever receive a document of that kind?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And my last question, General Skender. In view of the overall situation which you were very well acquainted with, tell me this, please, regardless of my military knowledge, would my commanding from the Main Staff, given the situation that we had, would it have succeeded in defending us from the Muslim offensive, or was it necessary to be on the spot, in the exact location to prevent a defeat -- our defeat by -- from the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: I think that given that you're on -- that when you were on the field it improved our effectiveness both in attack as well as defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And just my last question. When you were the commander of the operative zone, you had a car. Now, did you have a radio station in the car, or whatever, which enabled you to communicate directly with your operations officer in the zone or when we were dealing with the problem in Rama, for example, during those 48 hours, did you receive information as to what was going on in the -- on the Livanj battlefront facing the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: No. Every -- every time I went on the terrain with my SUV, my 4X4, I had no connection until I reached a place where the connection could be set up, either through a land-line or through the portable radio sets we had. But you know that these radio sets don't have a very large range.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Motorolas? Do you remember whether there were any Motorolas?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: These were Motorolas, but encrypted [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you, General Skender, for coming, and for answering my questions. And thank you, too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there is I think a mistake in the transcript. It says on line 16 of page 56, these were Motorolas, but encrypted, and I thought that the witness said the opposite, namely that they were open, they could be listened to by anyone. Maybe I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you're right. You're right. There were two types of Motorolas, scrambled ones, encrypted, and the normal Motorolas, but not everyone had a Motorola, those encrypted Motorolas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Skender.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could my binders be distributed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Skender, we met during the proofing session; right? And we discussed the documents that I'm going to put before you now, but I'd just like to go back for a moment to a question that General Praljak asked you about what kind of information you received from the ground, from the field, and can -- am I correct in saying that the only written information was received from about the 20th of December, 1993, when you became the commander of the military district of Tomislavgrad? Would that be correct? Is that the period you meant?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Yes. Before that period of time I had no command authority and no one was dealing with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Skender, I'm going to ask you now to take a look at my binder, the pink one, and -- open it and look at the first document. You have it in front of you, and it's a report, your report, and I'm sure you'll recognise it. And the number of that report is 2D3045.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll just say briefly that this is a report on combat readiness, that's the title, of the Tomislavgrad Military District, and your signature is on the first page. The date is the 24th of February, 1994, and it is being sent to the HVO Main Staff of Posusje to the commander personally. Now, Mr. Skender, we have your signature on your first page, and during the proofing session I showed you this report. Now, can you then confirm that it is indeed a report which you compiled -- or let me ask you first, did you sign it? Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Yes, I signed this report, but it was drafted by the officers in charge of their areas, by each of the officers in charge of their areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Skender, were they your assistants for the individual areas within the frameworks of the operative zone -- or, rather, in the Tomislavgrad Military District?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Yes, these were officers of my staff, of the Tomislavgrad Operational Zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It's been a long time, Mr. Skender, many years since this report was drafted, but you have seen it, and you had a chance to read through it in detail during the proofing session. So can you now remember and tell us whether you had an insight into the situation as it is described and written down in this report, and do you today confirm that that was what the situation was like as it is presented here?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel adjust her microphone, please, and speak into it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The situation was as it is presented in this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Skender, I'm going to ask you now -- well, I'll try and get through this as quickly as possible, get through the report, focusing on parts of your statement and your testimony here today and your answers to some of the questions you were asked during the examination-in-chief. For us to do so, let's turn to page 2. It's 2 in the Croatian, and it has a number 1 at the top. So all those looking at the English translation, I'd like to draw your attention to the numbers at the top of each page. Under number 1, this is what it says in the report, Mr. Skender: "The training and qualification at all layers of command and control is not at the required level for successfully carrying out combat activities. The reasons are generally known: due to a deficiency of educated staff, regular soldiers have been assigned to the aforementioned commanding positions -- or, rather, to formational commanding positions, to formational commanding positions of squads as well as establishment positions and posts in the commands of the brigades and military districts. "There are few former JNA officers, reserve officers and non-commissioned officers occupying commanding positions." Mr. Skender, does that part of your report in fact reflect the situation with the command staff at the -- in the HVO at this time, which is February 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: I can't say what was happening at the command of the HVO, but there were problems with the commanding officers, including commanding officers in my own operational zone. There were people who had received no military training at all but who were appointed just because no one else volunteered for the position.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Skender, you therefore confirm that that's what the situation was like on the territory on which you were the commander, that is to say the Tomislavgrad Military District, but what I want to ask you is about the period before, when you travelled the HZ HB, did you come across similar situations in other areas where you travelled? And I'm referring to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and from July -- you were there from July 1993, and you moved around this general area.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: This same situation prevailed elsewhere, if not worse.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you now, on that same page, before we come to the section titled "Conclusion," to look at the fourth line in the previous paragraph, and you are listing some of the main problems in the military district, and you say units are not up to strength, and even without the necessary weapons and ammunition, winter clothing, artillery support, communication equipment. Now, on page 17, lines 3 to 6, you said that the situation was catastrophic and that the units were not supplied well enough, didn't have the necessary resources. Now, could you explain to the Trial Chamber what this 1BK means and why it says here: "Even without 1BK." What is this BK that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: BK is equipment, is the number of ammunition per man. Each man is supposed to have a number of rounds for his assault rifle. It's a standard issue. If he don't have the standard issue, he must be resupplied, and it could be a problem, of course, because he's coming to the front and he's -- to the front line. If he's coming without any rounds in his -- for his assault rifle, there's going to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Skender, can you tell the Trial Chamber whether there were any standards in place in the army or in armies, the armies that you were in, generally speaking, standards, well-known standards, on how many combat sets were necessary when an offensive was under way or when some military action was under way? Is there any difference between how many combat sets you need when you're on the defensive and how many combat sets you would need when you were on the offensive?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: In each army there's a standard issue per weapon. For the French Army, for example, it's a hundred rounds for an assault rifle. But when you are in an offensive operation or even sometimes a defensive operation, each man may receive one or two additional standard issues, as far as rounds are concerned, to make sure that the combat can continue, because the main problem during combat is the logistics. Once the combat's under way, if soldiers run out of rounds they need to be resupplied and that takes time. After that, it's too late.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I was asking you, because of the standards. And from your report, what happens is that your soldiers would turn up without a single combat set. You didn't have it at your disposal. You didn't have these combat sets or weapons at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Yes. Often soldiers would arrive with a weapon but no ammunitions, which is proof once again of the very poor command of this unit. Any commander who hasn't checked beforehand that the soldier is fully equipped with clothes -- clothing and ammunitions before sending him to the front, I mean is responsible for this very poor situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me take the opportunity of this question to ask you a follow-up question. It's absolutely essential, as far as I'm concerned anyway. You just told us that the soldiers were arriving with a rifle but no rounds for their rifle and so forth and so on. So let's start from this: When you were in command, when offensives were under way or possibly defensive operations were under way but had already been planned because you knew that the others were going to attack, could you tell us whether automatically a written order is issued, written order which is sent throughout the chain of command to say at this day, this hour, this area, this operational zone there's going to be an attack. This is what is required, with a list. I would like to know whether each operation is accompanied by a written order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You need a written order, because -- you need that to get the ammunitions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the military rule throughout the world, but I would like to know whether this military rule applied also to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's true that in the HVO many things happened just with verbal orders only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were there military operations conducted with only verbal orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There's always been a written order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, you have 15 minutes before we are finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. If I don't get through all my questions, I would like to carry on on Monday. Now, I'd just like to put something right. Ms. Alaburic drew my attention to it. On page 61, line 17, it says about this combat set that we're talking about "standard issue" and it should say "combat set." "Combat set" is the term that we see in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, you said a moment ago, Mr. Skender, that if there wasn't -- weren't enough weapons -- if an army didn't have enough weapons up at the front line that this was one of the problems of command and that the commander should check this out and verify if they had everything they needed, but can you tell us whether you know -- whether there exist -- whether there was enough ammunition and weapons generally in the HVO HZ HB logistics for each commander to be able to receive as much weapons and ammunition as his men needed?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: The HVO had enough ammunition for the assault rifles. If men arrived at the front line without any ammunition, it was because they had left the ammunitions home, and their direct commander didn't check that they had their ammunitions with them. There was hardly any control. When men left the combat zone, there was no check as to whether -- how many ammunitions left the zone. And there were hardly any checks either on the incoming ammunitions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Skender, we'll look through the documents and see if that was the actual situation as you saw it, but let's take this step-by-step. Staying with the report, let's look at page 4. Page 4 the last paragraph it says: "The average number of men in the units does not exceed 30 per cent in any of the units." Can you confirm that that was what the situation was at the time? "The average strength of the military occupational specialties in the units does not exceed 30 per cent." Is that how it was in Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: It doesn't have anything to do with the number of men, but there are speciality. In other words, there was only 30 per cent of the men that had the required speciality in a particular unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's what I had in mind. Now, moving on to the following page, page 5, let's see what the establishment strength was of the units. And we have a table there where we see the number of officers, the establishment strength, the actual strength, and the percentage. And can you explain what this means to the Trial Chamber? What does all this mean?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: There is in any army an allowance for the officers, non-commissioned officers, and the military of that form a unit. An allowance. That is the theory. In practice, we have the facts on the ground. In other words, the unit is then supplemented by a given number of officers, non-commissioned officers, and soldiers. This is how you can work out the number or percentage of men in these units.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's take a look at section 5, logistic support, and it says there towards the end of the page: "The electricity on the floor where logistics works fails as soon as it starts to rain." And there's another observation made there, "the ratio between civilian structures and the command for the military district, which is unbearable. The attitude of the civilian structures towards the command of the ZP is unbearable." Now, we saw that the building where the -- where logistics was put up was not adequate or suitable, and then you say that the attitude of the civilian structures towards the command was unbearable. Could you explain that, please? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: You need to know that all commands, including mine, were installed in civilian buildings. Mine was in a former factory, and these buildings were often quite old buildings. Work needed to be done on these buildings. Large-scale improvements needed to be made. For instance, the logistics section was located in an area of a building when -- where whenever it started raining they got wet. So that was an inappropriate location to work in good conditions. It was too expensive to repair, and since the state had no money, this did not get repaired.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And tell me, Mr. Skender, why was this observation made about the relationship with the civilian structures and the command, and it says that they were unbearable. So can you think back and try and remember why you wrote this and what the situation was like?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, because every time the military settled somewhere, we were in the way. That's the first thing. And secondly, it is true that the military destroyed a lot of the equipment and the houses. So the civilians were not too happy about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to look at page 7 of this report of yours now, please. And on that page you speak about the quartermaster's corps, and I'd like to draw your attention to the food supply, and you say that food supply is coming from Grude, from the central logistics base, the SLOB. What was this SLOB Grude?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Grude was the logistics centre of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So it says here that the food was good and there was a variety but in insufficient quantities and that the percentage of delivered food was just 80 per cent, which sometimes causes problems in its distribution. Do you remember that and the problems that you faced?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Of course I remember, because my command and I, well, very often we didn't have enough to eat.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, going further down the page, we see that it says that beds were urgently required in order to put up the soldiers, and then it says at the end that certain responsibilities had to be fulfilled but they didn't have the wherewithal; that is say, that the army didn't have enough beds for the accommodation of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: That's right. There wasn't enough accommodation and beds were in short supply, because there were a great number of units that weren't properly accommodated. I asked for more beds, which is a prerequisite for a soldier when he's not in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a little bit surprised about this bed question, because we've been told at length several times that the HVO soldiers were not usually in the barracks. They went home when they weren't on the front line, and at home we can assume that they had beds. So you are discussing a situation which seems to be different here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We need to place this in context. We were located behind a mountain. There was only Prozor there and the forest. The units that arrived on the front line comprise a set number of soldiers, of reserve soldiers, that were not on the front line, and these had to be accommodated somewhere. They were not in a barracks because there weren't any barracks. So it was important to find places. In our case it was in a building, to find a place to stay for these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you to ask you to look at the next document now, please, which P1077, in the pink binder. It's the next document. Have you found it? It's a document signed by Mr. Bruno Stojic, and it is on an appointment. And I'd like to ask for your comments, and at the beginning of your report -- well, when you refer to your report, you say that -- that the establishment posts -- that there weren't trained cadres for the establishment posts and that ordinary soldiers were assigned to those posts. So may we have your comments on that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: This only confirms what I have said already. People were appointed to a command post without any military knowledge whatsoever that goes with it, either via of political collection -- connection. I don't know. A corporal was, for instance, appointed commander of a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Skender, we're talking about the deputy commander here, not the commander. It's the deputy commander who is mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Yes. Assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And I consider this to be an important point, and I refer to what you say in your report, because in your report you're not talking about private connections. In your report you say that the reasons for acting in this way are common knowledge because there were no trained officers, and that is why ordinary soldiers were appointed to establishment posts of commanders and lance corporals and so on, that they were appointed to these posts although they didn't have the necessary qualifications in terms of establishment and rank. It should have been a colonel here, whereas we see there was a reserve lance corporal assigned to the post. Am I right when I say that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. He was appointed colonel and second in command, and this was obvious in two ways. Either he got there through his connections or there was nobody else to fill this position, which was unfortunately quite often the case. So someone got appointed, someone who had been chosen by the people in the brigade either because the person was a pal or he was well-built or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we shall stop for today. Ms. Nozica will resume on Monday, and on Monday Ms. Alaburic will finish her cross-examination, and then the Prosecutor will cross-examine you. We shall meet again on Monday at a quarter past 2.00. In the meantime, I wish everyone a pleasant evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 28th day of September, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.00 p.m.,
